opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it is honestly just practice. I've broken a lot of defenses at this point, and after you've done it enough times you start to see the same patterns over and over. Someone proposes a defense, and you read the paper, and somewhere in there there's a sentence that makes you go, "Huh, that's a little weird." Maybe they evaluated against an attack that wasn't designed for their defense, or there's some component that makes gradients hard to compute, or the robustness numbers are just a little too good. Those little moments of "that's strange" are usually where the problem is.

The other part is having the right mindset. When you build a defense, you're naturally thinking about all the ways it works. When you attack, you have to assume it's broken and ask, "If this were broken, how would it be broken?" You're not trying to prove it's secure. You just need one way through. That changes how you read everything.

I also try to treat each attack as a learning exercise. After I break something, I'll go back and ask: what was the actual reason this failed? Was it something specific to this defense, or a general lesson? Most of the time the lesson generalizes. Gradient masking, for example, showed up in a huge number of defenses that looked totally different on the surface but failed for basically the same reason. Once you internalize a few of those core failure modes, a new defense often stops looking new. It's one of maybe five or ten things you've seen before.

And then, honestly, a lot of it is just being willing to do the tedious work. People imagine there's some brilliant flash of insight, and sometimes there is, but more often it's running the code, stepping through it, printing out intermediate values, and noticing that something isn't behaving the way the authors said it would. The intuition is mostly built out of having done that grinding many, many times.

r002.rationale: It describes adopting an attacker’s mindset and looking for a way through, but does not identify discerning how defenses can be broken as Carlini’s comparative advantage.

r003.rationale: The response says experience reveals recurring failure patterns and that new defenses often match failure modes seen before, such as gradient masking.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm not sure it's intuition so much as a habit of mind. A lot of it comes from spending years looking at defenses and noticing that they tend to fail in the same few ways.

The first thing I do when I see a new defense is ask: what does this actually assume about the attacker? Almost every defense has some implicit model of what the adversary is going to do. Maybe it assumes the attacker will use gradients, or that the perturbation will look a certain way, or that the attacker only gets one shot. The attack usually lives in the gap between what the defense assumes and what the adversary is actually allowed to do. If the paper says "we are robust to adversarial examples," I translate that in my head to "we are robust to the specific attack we ran," and then I ask what else is permitted under the threat model.

The second thing is that I try very hard not to be clever too early. People imagine that breaking defenses requires some deep insight, but most of the time the first thing I do is just run the simplest possible attack, properly. A lot of defenses fall to that. The failure is often on the evaluation side rather than the defense side. The authors ran an attack, it didn't work, and they stopped. They didn't check whether the attack was actually optimizing anything, whether the gradients were informative, whether the loss was even going down. So I look for signs that the evaluation was broken: a defense that gets stronger when you increase the attack budget, or accuracy numbers that are suspiciously close to clean accuracy. Those are red flags that something in the pipeline is masking the real behavior.

Third, I think about the defense as a mechanism, not a result. What does it do to the input, what does it do to the gradient, where does the signal get lost? If a defense works by randomizing something, I ask whether I can average over the randomness. If it works by making gradients useless, I ask whether I can get a useful gradient from a surrogate or just do a gradient-free search. If it detects adversarial inputs, I ask whether I can add the detector to my loss and attack both at once. Once you've seen a dozen defenses, you start to recognize that most of them are variations on a handful of ideas, and each idea has a corresponding counter.

And then there's a mindset piece, which is probably the closest thing to intuition. You have to actually want the defense to fail. Not in a mean-spirited way, but you have to approach it as if you're the adversary and you have all the time in the world. If I'm the attacker, I'm not going to politely stay inside the box the defender drew. I'm going to read the code, I'm going to find the part the authors didn't think about, I'm going to try things that feel stupid. Being willing to try the stupid thing is underrated.

The last piece is just time and persistence. When I say a defense is broken, that usually means I spent a few days on it, not a few minutes. People sometimes think breaking a defense is a quick thing, and occasionally it is, but more often it's running experiment after experiment, reading the implementation closely, and slowly building a picture of why the attack isn't working yet. The intuition, if there is one, is mostly knowing which direction to keep pushing when the first ten things don't work.

r002.rationale: It describes how Carlini looks for ways to break defenses, but does not identify this as a comparative advantage over others.

r003.rationale: It says years of examining defenses reveal recurring failure modes, and that new defenses often match variations of familiar ideas and counters.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it is pattern recognition from trying things and seeing what breaks. You develop a sense for when a defense is actually removing a capability versus when it’s just making one particular way of accessing that capability harder.

When I look at a defense, I try to ask: what assumption is this relying on? Maybe it assumes that the attacker will ask a question directly, or that the malicious instruction will look different from ordinary text. Then the interesting question is whether I can violate that assumption while still accomplishing the thing I wanted to do.

And I think the intuition is useful for deciding where to look, but you shouldn’t trust it too much. I can have a very compelling story for why an attack should work, and then it doesn’t. Or something that seems almost too simple works surprisingly well. You have to run the experiment. The intuition gives you hypotheses; the actual behavior of the system tells you whether you were right.

r003.rationale: The response explains intuition as pattern recognition built by trying things and observing what breaks, then applying that experience when examining a defense.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it is developing a feel for where the assumptions are. When someone proposes a defense, I try to understand why they think it works. What is it assuming the attacker can do? And then, more importantly, what is it assuming the attacker won’t do?

A defense might work very well against the particular attacks that were used to evaluate it. But that doesn’t necessarily mean it has removed the underlying vulnerability. So I try to distinguish between something that makes an attack harder to find and something that actually prevents the attack.

And then there’s a lot of experimentation. You try something, it fails, and you look at how it failed. That gives you a little more information about the system, and you use that to decide what to try next. The intuition is useful for choosing where to look, but ultimately you have to turn it into an attack that works.
